# Labour Party Manifesto 2017 Summary: "For the Many, Not the Few"

This manifesto presents Labour's vision of Britain transformed through collective investment and genuine democratic control, challenging what it describes as a rigged economic system that benefits the wealthy few at the expense of ordinary working people.

## Economic Philosophy

Labour rejects the Conservatives' austerity approach, arguing that seven years of cuts have created falling living standards, shrinking public services, and deepening inequality. The party positions itself as understanding that wealth creation is a collective endeavour between workers, entrepreneurs, investors, and government—each deserving a fair share of rewards.

The manifesto commits to a fully costed programme to "upgrade our economy," establishing a £250 billion National Transformation Fund for infrastructure investment whilst maintaining fiscal responsibility through the "Fiscal Credibility Rule"—balancing day-to-day spending while borrowing prudently for investment.

## Taxation and Public Services

Labour pledges that 95% of earners will face no income tax increases, with only the top 5% asked to contribute more. The party promises to combat tax avoidance while protecting small businesses from excessive burdens.

Central to Labour's vision is creating a National Education Service—"cradle-to-grave" free education including abolished university tuition fees, restored maintenance grants, and expanded childcare provision. The NHS would receive £30 billion additional funding, with commitments to end privatisation and restore it as a truly public service.

## Workers' Rights and Ownership

The manifesto presents extensive workplace reforms: banning zero-hours contracts, ending the public sector pay cap, raising minimum wage to £10 per hour, repealing the Trade Union Act, and introducing sectoral collective bargaining. Labour would shift the burden of proof against bogus self-employment and create a new Ministry of Labour.

Crucially, Labour proposes widening economic ownership through doubling the cooperative sector, giving employees "right to own" when companies are sold, and returning privatised utilities to public ownership—railways, energy, water, and Royal Mail—arguing privatisation has failed to deliver for consumers.

## Housing and Social Security

Recognising a housing crisis of supply and affordability, Labour commits to building over one million new homes, including 100,000 council and housing association homes annually. Private renters would receive rent controls and three-year tenancies; the bedroom tax would be scrapped.

The social security system would be rebuilt with dignity at its core—scrapping punitive sanctions, increasing disabled people's support, and implementing the UN Convention on Rights of Persons with Disabilities into UK law.

## Brexit and International Relations

Labour accepts the referendum result but rejects the Conservatives' approach, prioritising jobs and living standards through maintaining benefits of the Single Market and Customs Union. The party commits to protecting workers' rights, environmental standards, and immediately guaranteeing EU nationals' rights.

Internationally, Labour emphasises multilateral diplomacy over unilateral intervention, maintaining defence spending at 2% of GDP whilst pursuing nuclear disarmament, and continuing 0.7% development aid spending. The party would recognise Palestine and appoint ambassadors for women's rights, LGBT rights, and religious freedom.

## Democratic Reform

Labour proposes a Constitutional Convention examining fundamental reform of how Britain works, reducing voting age to 16, democratising the House of Lords, and genuinely devolving power to communities rather than concentrating it in Westminster.

Throughout, the manifesto frames this programme as restoring the post-war settlement's promise—that collective investment and democratic control can deliver prosperity, security and dignity for all, not just the privileged few.
